question: How does the 2024 global coral bleaching event compare with earlier mass bleaching events?

answer.text:
The global coral bleaching event confirmed on **April 15, 2024** was the **most widespread on record**. It began in early 2023 and likely ended in mid-2025. NOAA documented mass bleaching in at least **83 countries and territories** across the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. ([coralreefwatch.noaa.gov](https://www.coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/research/coral_bleaching_report.php))

| Global bleaching event | Share of global reef area exposed to bleaching-level heat stress |
|---|---:|
| 1998 | ~21% |
| 2010 | ~37% |
| 2014–2017 | 68.2% |
| **2023–2025** | **84.4%** |

That’s about **16 percentage points above the previous record** and roughly **four times the area exposed in 1998**. The heat was also unusually intense: NOAA added three levels to its bleaching alert scale to distinguish higher risks of mass coral death. ([icriforum.org](https://icriforum.org/4gbe-2025/?utm_source=openai))

**Heat exposure isn’t the same as coral death.** Bleached corals can recover if temperatures fall soon enough. Even so, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network estimated that global hard coral cover fell **8.9% relative to its 2023 level** in just one year—the largest single-year drop on record. That estimate does not include the event’s full toll in 2025. The longer-term concern is that increasingly frequent marine heatwaves are giving reefs less time to recover between events. ([natureseychelles.org](https://natureseychelles.org/~documents/international-and-regional-documents/status-of-coral-reefs-of-the-world-2025/?layout=file))
